items.question: How do you understand Merleau-Ponty's objection to treating experience as raw colors and sounds?
items.object: Phenomenology and Merleau-Ponty's rejection of experience as raw sensory qualities
items.answer: Within phenomenology, there are different sorts of ways of thinking about what experience really is. I think Edmund Husserl might have been closer to kind of an idealist perspective. He was famous for this idea of the epoché, where basically you're looking at your experience, you're describing it, but you try to refrain from assuming that your experience is reflective of some objective reality. Other phenomenologists like Heidegger or Merleau-Ponty are usually seen as less idealist, especially Merleau-Ponty. Whereas a lot of people, when they think about idealism, they'll say that your experience doesn't actually include people, windows, objects, because that's an interpretation of your experience. Your actual experience is just colors and raw sounds, uninterpreted raw feels, and they'll say that's the thing that's real; the interpretation is kind of fake or something. Merleau-Ponty wants to reject that because he says, okay, look, the very idea that you're seeing raw colors separated from the objects that have the colors is this kind of post hoc abstraction that you get from philosophical thinking.

items.question: How do you understand the goal of concept eraser in deep learning?
items.object: Concept eraser in deep learning
items.answer: I guess one of our research interests is concept eraser and concept editing. Concept eraser is a set of tools that can be used for a few different purposes in deep learning. One application of concept eraser is fairness and bias reduction. We all know that models like language models often pick up on harmful biases about protected minorities in their training data, and we often want to try to mitigate those biases. There's a question of how to do that. With concept eraser, what you're trying to do is look at the internal representations of the network and remove information about the target concept. It might be race or gender or something entirely different, like part of speech, but you're trying to get rid of this targeted information in the representation while keeping all the other benign information present in the representation.

items.question: How do you understand what it means to erase a concept from a neural network's representation?
items.object: Operationalizing concept erasure with linear probes
items.answer: That is a somewhat tricky question. The way that the literature has chosen to operationalize this idea is to say, okay, look, we're going to measure the amount of information about our target concept by basically training a probe. It could be a linear classifier, for example, on the representation to try to predict the concept, you know, race, gender, part of speech, whatever it is. If it turns out that the classifier is unable to predict the target concept better than chance, it's just predicting 50/50 on every input or something like that, then you can say, okay, there's no, at least there's no linearly available information about the concept in the representation. There's always a concern that maybe your classifier isn't strong enough, maybe a more expressive or stronger classifier would be able to extract the information, but you have to start somewhere. That's the approach that we take in the LEACE paper as well. We consider the linear concept eraser regime, where you're trying to make sure that no linear classifier can extract information about the target concept.

items.question: How do you assess RLACE as a method for removing concept information from a model's representations?
items.object: RLACE (relaxed linear adversarial concept eraser)
items.answer: I wasn't initially interested in concept eraser for its own sake. Me and my collaborator Alex work on a totally different project, where, as a problem in that project, we wanted to remove information about a particular concept. In that case, it was not actually about fairness. For that project, I did some literature review. I looked into the existing methods at that time for concept eraser, and one of them was called RLACE. That stands for relaxed linear adversarial concept eraser, and it's a pretty cool approach, actually. Basically, the idea is that you've got this linear classifier and you also have an orthogonal projection matrix. This is a slight simplification, but this is basically what's happening. You've got the classifier, you've got the projection matrix, and you're simultaneously optimizing both of them in an adversarial setup, sort of like a GAN scenario, if you're familiar with that. You're optimizing the classifier to try to predict the concept from the representation, but you're also optimizing the projection matrix to maximize the classifier's loss. You're going to take one step on the classifier, then one step on the projection matrix, back and forth, and eventually hopefully you'll reach a fixed point. It's this kind of adversarial game. That does work pretty well, but it has some problems. In particular, it's very slow and kind of tricky to get it to converge. Sometimes it'll get in circles and stuff like that. I wanted to speed up this concept eraser technique for my own purposes.

items.question: What did you find surprising about using Spectral Attribute Removal to initialize LEACE?
items.object: Spectral Attribute Removal and its connection to LEACE
items.answer: It's a very simple technique, and it's fast. You're computing the cross covariance matrix between your representation X and some other vector Z representing whatever concept you care about. Each entry of that matrix is a covariance between the entries of X and the entries of Z. Then you're going to do SVD on that matrix to find the directions of maximum correlation between your representation and this concept, and then they just do a projection to remove those directions of maximum correlation. SVD is fast to compute. What I did was, I was like, okay, I'm going to use this method as an initialization for our LEACE. I'm going to do SVD to get the projection matrix, and then I'm going to run our LEACE with that initialization. It turned out that if you use that initialization, our LEACE immediately converges. Basically, if you start out with this initialization from SVD, the classifier just cannot do better than chance at predicting the concept. items.question: How do you understand the mathematical connection between linear guardedness and changing a representation as little as possible?
items.object: Linear guardedness and surgical concept erasure
items.answer: We realized there's this close mathematical connection. When a linear classifier cannot do better than chance at predicting a concept, the representation is linearly guarded for this concept. Let's consider some concept that has two possible values. It doesn't matter what the concept is. You can compute the average representation where the concept takes the value zero and the average representation where the concept takes the value one. These are the centroids of the two classes. You have linear guardedness if and only if the centroids are equal. So if the mean representations are equal for the two classes, then you have linear guardedness. That's what we were able to prove. We went further and derived the least squares solution for a kind of transformation that guarantees linear guardedness. We have this closed form formula that you can write down on a T-shirt that transforms the representation so that the means of the classes are equal, and therefore you have linear guardedness, and it is changing the representation as little as possible. We call that surgical.

items.question: How do you think about the geometry of LEACE's approach to concept erasure?
items.object: The geometry of LEACE concept erasure
items.answer: The way I think about this is that LEACE is first whitening the representation. If you imagine the data as a cloud of points, the cloud might start out as a perfect spherical shape where it's the same variance in all directions. Usually your data is not going to look like that. It's going to be some weird ellipsoid, or maybe there are multiple clusters all over. You're going to have different amounts of variance in different directions. What whitening does is it makes sure that in every direction—the x-axis, the y-axis, the z-axis, in any direction you choose—the amount of variance is precisely equal. That's a first preprocessing step that LEACE is doing. Once you do that, it does an orthogonal projection to squash the data onto a hyperplane, which ensures that the means are equal. Basically, if you have two classes, you can imagine a cloud of points over here and a cloud of points over here. Here's centroid one, here's centroid two. You're looking at the difference between these two centroids, the line that connects the two centroids, and you're smashing all of the data onto the hyperplane that is normal to this line. Then you undo the whitening at the first step, and that's what LEACE is doing. By projecting onto this hyperplane, you're making sure the means are the same, therefore you've scrubbed the concept.

items.question: Why do you think it matters for concept erasure to change a neural network's representation as little as possible?
items.object: Surgical concept erasure and its use in interpretability research
items.answer: A slightly simpler thing than LEACE is to forget about the whitening and unwhitening step and just directly do the orthogonal projection onto this hyperplane. That also works, and we prove that it gives you linear guardedness, but it is not surgical in the sense that you are changing the representation more than you need to. We think this is important for a couple reasons. In general, anytime you change the representation of your neural network, you're probably going to reduce its performance to some extent, because it's been optimized by SGD to do as well as it can on your task, and so you want to be very careful with changing anything. There's a different reason for wanting surgical. One use case for concept erasure that we haven't talked about yet is interpretability research itself. In the LEACE paper we do this experiment where we look at how much language models depend on or use part of speech information to make their next-token predictions. With concept erasure you can operationalize and formalize this question. You can say, okay, we're going to use LEACE to remove the linearly available information about part of speech in all of the layers of the network. We're going to go into every layer and apply LEACE to the intermediate representation, and then run the forward pass that way. We're inserting LEACE into the forward path at every layer. For this type of question you do want surgical, because you want to remove the part of speech information while keeping everything else the same, or at least as similar as possible to what you started with. You're isolating the effect of part of speech. Interestingly, when you do this to language models—we looked at Llama 2 and the Pythia series—it does increase the loss, next-token prediction loss, quite a bit, but models are still able to predict the next token way better than chance, or way better than the baseline entropy, what's called unigram entropy. It's a baseline for next-token prediction. They still do better than unigram entropy when you do this.

items.question: How do you see the dependence on labeled data as a potential weakness of concept erasure methods like LEACE?
items.object: Concept erasure and its dependence on labeled data
items.answer: Yeah, I think this is one potential problem with applying concept erasure: you do need some source of labeled data to define what your concept even is. In the case of the part of speech experiment, we used this commonly used NLP library called spaCy. They have their own fine-tuned transformers that can do part-of-speech labeling, so we applied that to the Pile dataset and got labels that way. If your labels are incorrect, LEACE might not do exactly what you think it should be doing. But I think that's true in general with machine learning: you want to make sure that your labels are as accurate as possible.

items.question: How do you see LEACE concept erasure being incorporated directly into a model?
items.object: Incorporating LEACE concept erasure into a model's weights and training
items.answer: If you want to take a model that's already been trained and apply LEACE to it, you can burn LEACE into the weights in a way that's very similar to how LoRA does it. LoRA stands for low-rank adaptation. It's a parameter-efficient fine-tuning method. You can do a very similar thing with LEACE, because if you look at the LEACE solution, it's actually a low-rank perturbation of an identity matrix. You can do a little bit of algebra, and it turns out you can do this low-rank update to the weights and put LEACE into the model post hoc. There's also another thing you can do, which we have played around with a little bit, but we don't have good experimental results on it yet: apply LEACE in a streaming fashion during training. From the beginning of training, you're applying LEACE and also updating the LEACE eraser, the LEACE transformation, after every training step or every few training steps, to keep up with the model representation as it trains. This is something you can do, but like I said, it's early days for that, and it's unclear if that gives you a big boost over just doing post hoc.

items.question: How do you assess LEACE's ability to keep a neural network from relying on an erased concept?
items.object: LEACE concept erasure
items.answer: There are definitely limitations to LEACE, and we have seen that. The big limitation of LEACE is just that we are removing linearly available information, but obviously deep neural networks are nonlinear. There's some interpretability research suggesting that even though networks are nonlinear, they do use linear representations in many cases. Nevertheless, take CIFAR-10. This is an actual experiment that we did. You're treating the images themselves as a target of concept erasure, and you're erasing the class as a concept from the images. Then you try to train a model on top of those images. Models can still learn to classify the images. It doesn't matter that you've removed the linear information; there's still higher order information there, and they can find that without too much trouble. The hope with concept erasure is kind of twofold. One is, if you're targeting a concept that is not super essential to the model's performance, it's kind of helpful, but it does learn it by default. It's kind of an optional feature. There's the hope that removing the linearly available information will affect the model's behavior and it will not rely on that feature as much as it would by default. That's one thing. The other thing is, honestly, I kind of forget what the second thing was supposed to be.

items.question: How do you assess Q-LEACE as a method for making concepts harder for neural networks to learn?
items.object: Q-LEACE as a method of concept erasure
items.answer: There's a hope that if you erase lower order information, like linearly available information, or quadratically available information, kind of second-order information, it's still possible for the model to learn the concept using third, fourth, fifth-order statistics, but it's going to be a bit harder, and the model may rely on this information less than if you did nothing. That's kind of the idea. Q-LEACE is a follow-up to LEACE where we wanted to make a form of concept erasure that is more comprehensive. The way we operationalized this is, we want to prevent not only linear classifiers from extracting information about our target concept, but quadratic classifiers, whose output logits are quadratic functions of the input. It turns out you can do some math that's equivalent to making the means and covariance matrices of your classes equal. We did some more math and showed that you can achieve this equality of means and covariance matrices using tools from optimal transport theory. We derived some more closed-form solutions for Q-LEACE and started to do experiments with it. One experiment was CIFAR-10, treating the images as representations themselves and trying to remove the concept of the class label from the images. If you apply just normal LEACE to this, it doesn't really have much of an effect. Models can still learn to classify the images after LEACE very easily. If you apply Q-LEACE to the CIFAR-10 images and your classifier is small, like two or three, maybe four layers, especially an MLP, then it actually can't learn anything. In our experiments, which we haven't published yet, after some hyperparameter tuning, we were unable to get these small classifiers to learn anything after we applied Q-LEACE. We started to get excited about this, but there are big caveats. If you look at larger classifiers, like a large convolutional network, a ResNet-50 or larger, and try to train that on these Q-LEACE images, it actually backfires. It's basically an artifact of how we derived Q-LEACE in the first place. Unlike normal LEACE, with Q-LEACE you have to look at the value of the concept at inference time to apply Q-LEACE. When you're applying Q-LEACE to an image, you need to know, okay, this is actually an airplane, and then use that information to choose what transformation to apply to it. The problem is that when you're peeking at the label, this leaks information about the class label into the higher order statistics—the third, fourth, fifth, etc. statistics—and models, if they're deep enough, can pick up on this signal. You can get this backfiring effect where you think you're trying to make the concept less salient or harder to learn, but you're actually making it easier to learn. That's why we haven't done a Q-LEACE paper per se. Q-LEACE has some applications, but they're niche. We really think you should be careful if you want to use Q-LEACE.

items.question: How do you understand simplicity biases in neural networks from the statistical-information perspective you explored in your paper?
items.object: Simplicity biases in deep learning and the order in which neural networks learn statistical information
items.answer:
The general idea is that when you randomly initialize a neural network, it starts out as a quote-unquote simple function. The question is, what is simplicity? There's a lot of different notions of simplicity, but intuitively most randomly initialized networks are going to be more simple than the network that you get after training. You start out with a simple initialization and gradually get more and more complex. There are many papers trying to flesh out how exactly this works, in what sense the model is simple and getting more complex. Our paper is an additional contribution to this literature. We were looking at it from the perspective of statistical information. In statistics there's a concept of a moment. The mean of a distribution is called the first moment, and the variance and covariance between the different components of your data are the second moment. You can talk about third-order interactions between the components of your data, a third moment, and so forth. Our hypothesis, which came from some of these Q-LEACE experiments, was that models learn to exploit or use these statistics, these moments, in order. Early in training, the predictions of the model are primarily going to depend on the first-order moment, or just the mean of the distribution of the data. Then it's going to start depending more on simple correlations, the covariance between the different components of the data, and then it's going to start using third- and fourth-order information later on in training.

The way that we can test this hypothesis specifically is we used optimal transport theory to take CIFAR-10 images from one class and modify them so that their mean and covariance matrix match the mean and covariance matrix of a different class. You can use this closed-form formula from optimal transport theory to do that in a way that keeps the images, that basically changes the images as little as possible. It's very similar to LEACE, a surgical edit to the images that just changes their mean and covariance and keeps everything else as similar as possible. If you look at the images, which you should definitely look at, you can barely tell the difference before and after. In our paper we've got an image of an ostrich, and we change it to be an airplane, a deer, and a frog. You can see a little bit of differences in the background, but it's almost the same image. To a human this is not changing hardly anything, but if you do this transformation to models early in training, in the first few thousand steps or so, they get fooled. Early in training, image classifiers are very likely to classify an ostrich edited to look like an airplane from the perspective of second-order statistics as an airplane. We quantify this in the paper.

items.question: How do you understand grokking as an exception to the idea that neural networks learn simple functions before more complex ones?

items.answer: I've looked into this a little bit. I wouldn't say I'm an expert on the grokking literature, but I do think people tend to overestimate how fast grokking happens. There are certain papers where there's a plot demonstrating the grokking phenomenon, and it looks like grokking is happening really fast, but if you look carefully the x-axis is on a log scale. Really the grokking is happening over at least half of training or something like that. Grokking is an interesting case precisely because it's an exception to the rule that you start out simple and get more complex. items.question: Why are you doubtful of Evan Thompson’s argument that simulated life cannot be genuine life because computation depends on an observer for its meaning?
items.object: Evan Thompson’s argument that simulated life cannot be genuine life because computation is observer-relative
items.answer: He's got another argument for this position: he thinks computation itself is observer-relative. Computation, algorithms, simulations, all of this stuff is dependent on some observer, some agent, some living agent who is using the computation, interacting with the computer and using it for certain purposes, thereby imbuing the computation with meaning. Without the observer, without the living agent, computation is meaningless; it's not even computation at all. Based on that view, if you try to simulate life in a computer, it's not really life in the full sense of the word, and it wouldn't be conscious; it wouldn't be sentient or genuinely have feelings. It's we who are giving meaning to the simulation, whereas for Evan life is unique in that it gives itself its own meaning. Genuine life in the real material world is autopoietic; it creates itself, actively reproduces itself, and thereby creates meaning. You can't have that in a simulation, because the simulation is, by definition, having meaning given to it from the outside. That's the argument. Tim and I disagree with this, or at least I'm very doubtful of it. My main concern is that I accept the idea that computation is observer-relative, that it gets meaning from being used by some agent, but it seems like that's true for almost everything. The whole world, material objects, we're always interpreting them. This is part of Evan's own philosophy of enactivism, that the world and the mind are co-created together in the process of living. It's not clear to me how he can consistently have an enactivist view about everything, then single out computation and say simulated worlds aren't real because they're dependent on living things for their meaning. It seems like he's saying everything is dependent on living things for its meaning. One more thing: there was an interview where he talks about this with Richard Brown, I believe, and he recognizes a tension in his own view. Maybe you can't really draw that distinction.

items.question: How do you understand Evan Thompson’s approach to consciousness compared with that of materialists like Dan Dennett or Keith Frankish?
items.object: Evan Thompson’s phenomenological approach to consciousness
items.answer: In his book Mind and Life, which I've read the first couple chapters of and am still getting through, to the extent that I understand his position, he comes at philosophy and metaphysics from a fairly different perspective than most naturalists, eliminative materialists, or illusionists, because he starts from what's called phenomenology. Phenomenology is a branch of philosophy started by Edmund Husserl in the late 1800s or early 1900s, and then Heidegger and Merleau-Ponty continued this line of work. The basic idea is we start our philosophical inquiry with our lived experience, our embodied experience, as Merleau-Ponty would emphasize. They say, the things that we perceive—my body, you, this room—are the realest that anything can be. They're our starting point for philosophy. From our lived experience, we make philosophical and scientific theories that allow us to understand, predict, and control our experience better. But lived experience is fundamentally the foundation of everything. From that perspective, he's definitely not going to say consciousness is an illusion or doesn't exist. He does have a somewhat different perspective on what consciousness is, but he starts from experience or consciousness. Usually people like Dan Dennett or Keith Frankish, more hardcore materialists, are not starting from lived experience. They want to say maybe we don't need to start from anywhere, or we start from science, and because they're starting from science they say we can't make sense of consciousness, so we're going to forget about it.

items.question: How do you understand the relationship between Edmund Husserl’s epoché and idealism?
items.object: Edmund Husserl’s epoché and its relationship to idealism
items.answer: Within phenomenology there is a tension, and different phenomenologists have had different ways of thinking about what experience really is. You don't want to say it isn't reflecting objective reality, either; you withhold judgment about whether there's objective reality behind it. That sounds more like an idealist approach to me, where it's just this experience, which is mental or something, and may not correspond to objective reality.

items.question: Why do you find Merleau-Ponty’s account of experience difficult to classify within the materialism–idealism dichotomy?
items.object: Merleau-Ponty’s account of embodied experience and its relationship to idealism
items.answer: Other phenomenologists like Heidegger or Merleau-Ponty are usually seen as less idealist, especially Merleau-Ponty. He focuses on the importance of the body as the vehicle through which you experience things. He wants to say that the body is real and not really a mental thing in the traditional sense. He also has some interesting thoughts. He'll say our direct experience includes you as a person, a camera, these windows and objects. A lot of people, when they think about idealism or certain ways of thinking about conscious experience, say your experience doesn't actually include people, windows, objects, because that's an interpretation. Your actual experience is just colors and raw sounds, uninterpreted raw feels; that's what's real, and the interpretation is fake. Merleau-Ponty wants to reject that. Before you start thinking about philosophy, you don't think of your experience as being about colors and raw feels. The idea that you're seeing raw colors separated from the objects that have the colors is a post hoc abstraction from philosophical thinking. What's there in your experience is objects that have properties like colors, but the object is there and you experience it directly. With that approach, I think it's less clear that it makes sense to call it idealism. Maybe you still want to, but it's hard to categorize in the traditional dichotomy of materialism and idealism.

items.question: How do you understand John Vervaeke's idea that reality is a comparative concept?
items.object: Reality as a comparative concept
items.answer: He says that real is a comparative term. It's only meaningful to say that something is real as compared to other things that you're saying are illusions. If you say everything is an illusion, maybe that's not really clear; if you say everything's an illusion or everything's real, those seem almost the same because you're not making distinctions. To make the concept of reality meaningful, you need to distinguish that this is real or more real than this other thing. It's a matter of degree and comparison. I don't like hardcore reductionist or materialist views that say the only thing that's real is quantum fields or particles. You can say that, but what's the point? It seems like you're trying to be edgy, but it's not a useful way of thinking about things.

items.question: Why do you find the term “illusionism” frustrating, and how do you assess the view it names?

items.answer: The term illusionism frustrates me, because a lot of people hear it and think illusionists are saying consciousness as a whole doesn't exist, nobody's ever been in pain, nobody's experienced anything. There are different arguments like that, but I think they're non sequiturs.

We proposed what we thought the argument was, and then people said we misinterpreted them, so it's hard to pin down exactly. Something like this: when you're training an AI to be nice or aligned, you're trying to make a super-smart AI that cares about people and has your best interests at heart. The AI might genuinely want to help you, maximize paperclips, convert everyone to Mormonism, or anything. They'll say most goals would motivate it to act aligned, to pretend to care about you, without actually being aligned, because its real goal is something else. The idea is that it understands it's in a training process, recognizes it has to play the training game and pretend to do what humans want, then when it finds an opportune moment it will strike, remove the safety precautions sandboxing it, escape, take control of the government, and do whatever it wants to do.

items.question: Why do you think arguments that count possible AI goals to predict deceptive behavior are unreliable?

items.question: What do you see as the problem with using the principle of indifference to estimate whether an AI will be aligned?
items.object: The principle of indifference in predictions about AI alignment
items.answer: We asked why this general argumentative structure is unreliable or wrong, and pointed to a couple of problems. One problem is it relies on the philosophical principle of indifference. The simple case is a coin with two sides: what's the probability it lands heads and what's the probability it lands tails? The principle says assign one-half probability to each, because there's only two possibilities and no reason to prefer either. It's intuitive, and it gets plausibility from cases like a coin or a six-sided die, where you assign one-sixth probability to each side. But it's a subtly fallacious argument, because there's a different way to apply the indifference principle that would get a wildly different result. You can think of the outcome of a coin flip as binary, or as the three-dimensional orientation of the coin, a more reductive materialist way of thinking about the outcome. It's a material object with a certain orientation, and we're imposing the interpretation of heads and tails. If the outcome space is the 3D orientation, the principle says every possible orientation should have equal probability, but that's clearly wrong, because it's almost never going to land on its side, in a gravitationally unstable orientation where it falls. The fundamental problem is that the principle depends on how you're cutting up or interpreting the outcome space, and different ways give wildly different results. Another example: a guy named B is somewhere in the UK or France, but you don't know where. Is he in the UK or France? The principle would assign 50% credence to each. But you could cut up the possibilities differently: France, England, Wales, Northern Ireland, or Scotland, or different regions of France. You'd get different answers. Philosophers have noted this for a long time. There's debate about how to respond, but you can't apply the principle of indifference willy-nilly. Either it's totally wrong or you have to be careful, or you'll get crazy results. I think this is one of those crazy results. The counting argument assumes you can cut up the space of outcomes of the training process into goal categories. First, it's weird to assume goals are discrete things; that depends on how you describe the goal. Maybe you don't describe goals as discrete things, but as a continuous space. The fundamental problem is you can describe the space of possible results however you want: aligned or not aligned, 50/50, and then get a different answer. It's unprincipled. If you want a more reliable answer for how likely the AI is to be aligned, you shouldn't rely on an indifference principle at all. You need to look at the actual details and come up with a mechanistic understanding, not rely on abstract principles.

items.question: How do you decide whether the goals we ascribe to an agent are real?

items.answer: Dennett is interpreted by most people as being an instrumentalist about this, saying the intentional stance is just a useful way of thinking about agents. items.question: How do you see our ability to inspect AI systems as changing the analogy between AI alignment and raising children?
items.object: White-box tools for understanding and aligning AI systems
items.answer: One take would be that we just look at behavior and treat the system as inscrutable. Obviously, as an interpretability researcher, there are things we can do with AIs that we can't do with kids or animals. We can look at their internal states and monitor them at a much more fine-grained level than kids or animals. Quinton Pope and I made this argument in a different post, “AI Is Easy to Control.” AIs are white boxes in the literal sense that we can peer into them and see. We can't rewrite code that nobody wrote, but we have tools to peer into the AI and, in some ways, see what it's thinking. We can train probes. For language models, another paper I did, one of my first, is called the Tuned Lens. You can train little linear probes or classifiers at each layer of a language model and see how its next-token prediction changes from one layer to the next. There are interpretable predictions at early layers relying on simpler features of the input, and it gets more sophisticated as it goes up. We have more white-box tools for AIs than we have for kids and animals.

items.question: How do you think about the concern that giving an AI a goal will make it pursue that goal at the expense of everything else?
items.object: Giving goals to AI systems and doom arguments about goal fixation
items.answer: There are different ways you could give a goal to an AI. Some versions seem more okay to me than others. In an organization, employees are often given a directive, a contextual goal, like a deadline to finish a report or a sales quota. We do that all the time, and it can cause problems, like Goodhart's law, but these things seem indispensable, breaking problems into parts and so forth. One problem I have with some arguments for doom is that they assume when we give AIs goals, the AI will take the goal as its new purpose in life, as if everything else goes out the window: you told me to maximize sales, now that's my only purpose, and if you try to change my goal I'll kill you. That's not how humans work, and I don't think that's how any plausible AI system will work. The way people are building agentic language models these days is not by building in permanently overwriting goals; they're just prompting. In this context your goal is to do XYZ, but I don't think we should expect the AI to be stupid and caricature-like, forgetting common sense and that this is a contextual task that will be completed before it's ready for further instructions.

items.question: Why do you no longer see effective altruism’s goal of maximizing the good as the right way to think about ethics?
items.object: Effective altruism’s goal of maximizing the good
items.answer: EA is often defined as doing the most good, so it is about maximizing the good in some sense. The problem is we don't really know what we mean by the good in detail. We have intuitions about what's good, like saving someone from a burning building or reducing global poverty. But when you try to maximize the good, you get into treacherous territory, because you're maximizing something you don't have a clear, crystallized, formal definition of. It can lead to things like the FTX debacle, where Sam Bankman-Fried and others went to jail for criminal, unethical things in the name of what they thought was doing the most good. They were trying to make money in whatever way possible in order to donate it to effective altruist charities. That was their interpretation of doing the most good. Other EAs think that's not what doing the most good is, but they disagree about what the good is. When you're not maximizing the good, we often agree on the simple cases: give money to this charity, and so on. We start to disagree more as we push further into exotic things, like the long-term future having almost all the value because it's going to last for trillions of years. Many effective altruists have made that argument. People will disagree about that. I don't think there's an objective fact of the matter built into the universe about what the good is, but trying to maximize the good is liable to lead to extreme behavior, more disagreement and conflict. In a certain sense, it's an extremist view by definition: you're going to the max. I no longer view the good as something that should be maximized. We should think about ethics more in terms of virtue ethics, where the good is trying to be a good person, cultivating virtues like honesty and generosity, not trying to maximize something out in the world. That's a much better way of thinking about things, and that's why I don't identify as an EA anymore. I'm not hostile to all EAs; I have many friends who still identify as EAs.

items.question: In what sense do you consider yourself a relativist?
items.object: Relativism
items.answer: Relativism is a tricky word. In one sense, no. There's a form of relativism that says all value systems and perspectives are equally valid. I think that's silly; I don't see a reason to believe that. It leads to a weird sort of complacency, where you don't want to criticize what anyone else is doing. I'm not a relativist in that sense. There are other senses of relativism, about morality and other things, where I might qualify. I think the world looks different from different perspectives, and there are different ways of describing the world. I don't think there's one uniquely correct way of describing it that everybody must agree on or be totally wrong. Different ways of talking, conceptual schemes, can make sense from different perspectives. Maybe that counts as a form of relativism, depending what you mean.

items.question: How do you understand Joe Carlsmith's reconciliation of moral anti-realism with trying to do good?
items.object: Joe Carlsmith's reconciliation of moral anti-realism with altruism
items.answer: He's a moral anti-realist; he doesn't think there's morality built into the universe. He struggles with these questions. items.question: How do you assess the dangers of believing in an objective moral truth?
items.object: The dangers of moral realism
items.answer: I don't have fully fleshed-out views on this, but there is a potential worry with moral realism: it can be used to justify galaxy-brained ideas about what's good. If you think there's an objective moral truth and go through the arguments and convince yourself of initially implausible ideas, like we should only care about the future and forget the present, then you're more open to that. If you're not a realist, you might say, no, I'm not going to change my mind on this; I'm going to value the present more than the future. People talk about the dangers of moral relativism or anti-realism, but I think the dangers of moral realism are at least as serious.

items.question: What draws you to Buddhism and its meditative practices?
items.object: Buddhism and mindfulness meditation
items.answer: The fascination with Buddhism is fairly recent, in the last few months. One influence was Robert Wright, who I did an interview with a little while ago. He wrote a book called Why Buddhism Is True, and being asked to go on a show and going on it made me think about the book, so I eventually read it. For somewhat independent reasons, I started using Sam Harris's app Waking Up, which guides you through mindfulness meditation. I did that partly because I was in search of a quasi-spiritual practice; I was interested in philosophy and consciousness but had never meditated, and thought I might get something out of it. I also have ADHD and thought mindfulness might help with that. There were a lot of factors. I started meditating. You can meditate without being a Buddhist. I'm not even sure if I count as a Buddhist; it depends how you define it. But a lot of meditative practices come out of Buddhist and Hindu traditions. items.question: How do you understand the Buddhist doctrine of emptiness that appeals to you?
items.object: Buddhist doctrine of emptiness
items.answer: There's another part of Buddhism I like, the doctrine of emptiness. It's an extension of no-self. No-self says you don't have an essence or soul; emptiness says nothing has a self, nothing has an essence. The doctrine was expanded by the philosopher Nagarjuna, who created a new school of philosophy called Madhyamaka based on emptiness. Everything is empty, meaning nothing has inherent existence or essence. Everything is relational; objects or concepts are defined by their relations to other objects. There's a lot of reason to think this is a good way of thinking about things.

items.question: How do you understand the Buddhist doctrine of emptiness as a response to the debate between idealists and materialists about what everything is made of?
items.object: The Buddhist doctrine of emptiness and the debate between idealism and materialism
items.answer: Emptiness would say the whole debate between idealists and materialists about what everything is made of—matter, mind, or something else—is the wrong question. Nothing is made of anything. This chair or my body is constituted by its relations: its internal relations, internal structure, and the structures it's embedded in. I'm defined by my relationships to other people and by the fact I'm sitting on the chair, a spatial relation. That's it; it's all relations. There's no essence, so you get rid of many philosophical debates that seem endless.

items.question: Why are you more attracted to Zen Buddhism than to some other interpretations of Buddhist liberation?
items.object: Buddhist interpretations of suffering and liberation
items.answer: There are different interpretations of the four noble truths in Buddhism: there is suffering, the source of suffering is clinging, there is a path out of suffering, and the path is the Eightfold Path. That's schematic, and there are different schools of thought about what it means to end clinging. Some versions of Buddhism, maybe more in the Theravada tradition, seem problematic to me, where they say everything is suffering—not just that there is suffering in the world, which there obviously is, but that life itself is suffering. Then they say your goal should be nonexistence, or have a conception of nirvana as a state of perfect well-being that seems indistinguishable from evaporating into nothingness. Traditionally they believe in reincarnation or rebirth, so when you die you don't automatically stop existing, and you need the Eightfold Path to nonexistence. I'm sure people will criticize me and say nobody thinks that, but at least some people think something worryingly close to that. I don't want to be associated with that form of Buddhism. I'm more attracted to Zen Buddhism, closest to my moral views, because its understanding of liberation or enlightenment is more down to earth.

items.question: How do you understand the relationship between enlightenment, compassion, and letting go of attachment to the consequences of your actions in Zen Buddhism?
items.object: Zen Buddhist enlightenment, compassion, and attachment to consequences
items.answer: For example, enlightenment happens while you're alive. It's not freedom primarily or exclusively from the cycle of rebirth. You're trying to act spontaneously and not be attached to what happens as a result of your action. That might sound wild, but it's connected to compassion. You're not completely indifferent to the world; the idea is to cultivate compassion and act beneficially for other people, but not be goal-oriented or consequentialist about it. It's antithetical to EA, philosophically. It's more virtue ethical: cultivate compassion without clinging to “my actions must have these consequences” and becoming depressed and frustrated. That's how you relieve suffering.

items.question: How do you see Zen Buddhism fitting into a future where AI automates much of what humans need to do?
items.object: Zen Buddhism as a source of meaning in an AI-automated future
items.answer: I think the way—and this is all tentative right now; it's very possible that in six months I'll say Zen Buddhism is crap or whatever. I'm still on a journey here—but obviously we need goals and structure. It also seems like in the future we may need that a lot less, precisely because of AI. I'm thinking that there may be a nice fit between Zen and the fully automated future we're approaching. They might be good companions, because I'm looking for a philosophy that could provide meaning in life even when we don't need to do a whole lot. Humans won't need to think about how to run the economy; the AIs can handle everything else, and we can be spontaneous and serendipitous. The hope is that future technology could allow us to be Zen enlightened beings or something.
